html:
The Tupinambá were the Tupi-speaking peoples who held much of the Brazilian coast when the Portuguese arrived in 1500, the landing of Cabral. They lived in large villages of longhouses, grew cassava, fished, and fought constant wars between villages, in which captives were ritually killed and eaten. They cut brazilwood for the first European traders in the brazilwood trade. Their language, Old Tupi, became the basis of the common language spoken across colonial Brazil.

The German Hans Staden, their captive in the 1550s, and French visitors to France Antarctique wrote about them, and their accounts fed Montaigne's essay "Of Cannibals". War, slavery and disease destroyed most coastal groups in the 1500s, as Portuguese Brazil grew.

The map's small territory is the land of the Tupinambá of Olivença in southern Bahia, a community that has reasserted its identity in recent decades and is seeking recognition of its land. See also Tupis.
